title: Bishop against knight: count the wings
outcomes: Predicts win or draw for bishop against knight positions that differ by one pawn's wing
States the rule of thumb (pawns on both wings favour the bishop) and a case where it fails
Sees that the rule does not carry over to opposite-coloured bishops

steps.text: In an ending of **bishop against knight**, the pawns often decide who stands better. A bishop reaches both wings in one move; a knight needs several. So pawns on **both wings** tend to favour the bishop, and pawns on **one wing** give the knight better chances to hold. This is a rule of thumb: test it on one position first.

steps.text: **When it holds.** The bishop's side has pawns on both wings, so the bishop can switch between them faster than the knight. **When it fails.** All the pawns on one wing: the knight can hold, as the next pair shows. Rule of thumb: count the wings before you count anything else. Opposite-coloured bishops follow other rules, so do not use this on them.

steps.title: Move one pawn
steps.prompt: White has a bishop and two pawns against a knight and a pawn, and the queenside pawn stands on the third rank. In the second position it has moved to the kingside, still on the third rank. In the third it has moved along its own wing. Predict each result, then check.
Which feature did you look at first: the wings, the passed pawn, or the colours of the bishops? Which did you forget in the position where you were wrong?
